listenings.text: The difference between people who read their notes and people who rehearse out loud is not preparation, because both groups prepare. It is where the difficulty happens. If you rehearse out loud, the difficulty happens in your kitchen, on a Sunday, with nobody watching, and it costs you nothing. If you only read, the difficulty is still ahead of you, and it will happen in the room, in front of the person you most wanted to impress. The sentences you have physically said before come out at a different speed. That is not confidence, it is mechanical. Your mouth has done the movement. So say it standing up, say it to the wall, say it badly the first three times, and then say it once more. The fourth one is the one you will use.

End of day one, debrief note. Two good things and one blocker. First, the booth conversations went far better than last year, and the reason is embarrassingly simple: I stopped opening with who we are and started opening with what we are working on this quarter. Three out of five people asked a follow-up question, which never used to happen. Second, the panel was a waste of ninety minutes and I should have left after fifteen, so tomorrow I park anything that is going to be published as a report. And the blocker. I still have no answer on the compliance side, which means the meeting on Thursday cannot close, so my priority in the morning is to find the person who owns it rather than chasing the person who has been apologising.

Somebody asked me what I would tell a person going to their first big conference, and my answer has changed over the years. I used to say prepare more. Now I say something quite different. Get one quick win in the first two hours. Any win. Ask one person a question and understand the answer. Say your own two sentences to somebody who does not care. Because what actually stops people at these events is not language and it is not knowledge, it is the belief, built in the first morning, that they are not going to manage. And that belief is beaten by evidence, not by preparation. One small thing that worked, early, and the rest of the week is a different week. I have watched it happen to a lot of people, including me.

paras: Every delegate at a large conference has prepared. Almost none of them have rehearsed, and the gap between those two words is where the whole week is decided.

Preparing means reading your own notes until they feel familiar. Rehearsing means standing up in your kitchen on a Sunday and saying the sentences out loud, badly, four times. The first three are uncomfortable and the fourth is the one you will actually use. The reason is mechanical rather than psychological: a sentence your mouth has physically produced before comes out at a different speed than one it has only read. Nobody who has done it once needs to be persuaded of this.

The dress rehearsal has a second function, which is to find the blockers while they are still cheap. Say your ninety seconds out loud and you discover, on your own sofa, that you do not actually know your own market penetration figure. Discover that at a stand and it is a different kind of afternoon. The same is true of the questions you cannot answer: a rehearsal turns them from an ambush into a contingency you have already planned for.

Then there is the week itself, which is a problem of bandwidth rather than ability. Four days, two hundred sessions and forty conversations is more than anybody can hold, so the useful skill is deciding what to park. Anything that will be published as a report: parked. Anything a colleague can cover: parked. What survives is short, and short is what makes it possible to debrief honestly at the end of each day, while it is still fresh, and to arrive on day two having changed something.

And there is one piece of advice that experienced delegates give more often than any other, which has nothing to do with language. Get a quick win in the first two hours. Ask one person one question and understand the answer. Say your two sentences to somebody who does not matter. What stops people at these events is rarely knowledge; it is a belief formed on the first morning that they are not going to manage. That belief is beaten by evidence, and the earliest evidence is the cheapest. The takeaway, from people who have done this for twenty years, is that the first small success is worth more than the last three hours of preparation.
